Over breakfast, the crew argued about what a pop song was really about and whether waitresses deserved a tip. Bram insisted the lyrics were about a dog, Cal said a woman, and Mr. Ash just shrugged, eating his eggs. Ren Vasco, fresh out of prison, sat silent, watching them bicker over coffee and toast.

Later, at the warehouse, Mr. Ash cradled Mr. Elm, who was screaming, his stomach wet with blood. “You’re not going to die,” Ash swore, pressing his jacket against the wound. Elm’s breath came in ragged gasps. Mr. Birch arrived, still shaking from the escape. “The job was a setup,” he said, his voice flat. “There’s an informer inside.” He hid the diamonds behind a loose brick outside.

Bram handed out tree aliases. Mr. Birch objected to being Mr. Birch. “It sounds stupid,” he said. Bram ignored him. Mr. Cedar strolled in, grinning, and produced a bound patrolman from the boot of his car—Doyle, a young cop in uniform.

Ren Vasco reported to Bram and Cal. They owed him for the years he kept his mouth shut. Bram nodded. “You’re Mr. Oak now.” Ren said nothing.

Left alone with Doyle, Mr. Cedar danced to an oldie on the radio, humming off-key. He cut off the cop’s ear with a hunting knife, then doused him in petrol. Doyle whimpered. Mr. Elm, lying on the floor, raised his gun and shot Mr. Cedar twice in the chest. Cedar crumpled. “I’m a cop,” Elm whispered to Doyle. “Police are waiting outside for Bram.”

---

Danny Roarke rehearsed a fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet. His handler Pruitt made him repeat it until he could tell it like a memory. “I was undercover, the guy pulled a knife—” “Again,” Pruitt said. Danny closed his eyes and let the words fall.

He performed the anecdote for Bram, his son Cal, and Mr. Ash. They laughed. Bram clapped his shoulder. “You’re Mr. Elm.” Danny smiled.

The robbery collapsed within a minute. Mr. Ash shot his way clear from the getaway car, Mr. Elm beside him, bullets sparking off the doorframe. Fleeing on foot, Elm hijacked a car. The terrified driver shot him in the stomach. Elm shot the driver dead, falling into the back seat. Ash drove the screaming Elm to the warehouse.

---

Cal returned, listened to Elm’s account of Cedar. He shot Doyle dead himself without a word. Bram arrived, looked at Elm, and said, “He’s the informer.” Mr. Ash refused to believe him, turning his gun on Bram. The three-way standoff ended in a blur of shots—Bram, Cal, Ash all hit. Only Ash and Elm still breathed.

Elm confessed. “I’m a police officer.” Ash shot him as the police stormed the warehouse. Ash was cut down by a dozen bullets, his body crumpling beside the man he had tried to save.

Lena Ward demanded that Wes Tarrow be killed. Aaron Vale bought a gun and tracked the man to a motel on the outskirts of town, his hands steady despite the alien pulse beating in his chest.

Three years earlier, Wes Tarrow had been newly born again. He held down a job at a lumber yard and coached boys’ baseball on weekends. His wife Nita watched him with dread—his fanaticism at the dinner table, the way his temper flickered behind his eyes when a kid missed a catch.

At the same time, Lena Ward was living a settled suburban life. She had recovered from addiction, married Doug, and raised two young daughters in a house with a white fence. She went to PTA meetings and baked cookies for the school bake sale.

Meanwhile, mathematician Aaron Vale was told his failing heart would kill him within weeks unless a donor was found. The doctor’s voice was calm, clinical, but the words landed like stones.

Lena went back to cocaine. She began methodically destroying herself—late nights, missed calls, the powder cutting through her veins like a promise.

One evening, Wes’s pickup hit Doug and both girls at a crossing. He drove off, then turned back, then fled again. The truck’s bumper was dented, the headlight shattered.

Before the accident, Aaron’s estranged wife Della had pressed him to agree to be inseminated with his frozen sperm. She wanted a child before he died. He had refused, then relented under her insistence.

At the hospital, Lena was told her husband and both children were dead. She stood in the hallway, the fluorescent lights buzzing, and the world went quiet.

Wes walked into a police station and confessed to the hit-and-run. He was sent back to prison, his born-again faith crumbling behind bars.

Doug’s heart was transplanted into Aaron, who woke up alive for the first time in months. The rhythm was foreign, a second hand ticking inside his ribs.

Unable to stop thinking about whose heart was beating in his chest, Aaron hired a private investigator to find the donor’s widow. The report came back: Lena Ward, now alone.

Released early, Wes walked out on Nita and on his faith. He took work at a motel far from home, cleaning rooms and staring at the highway.

Aaron followed Lena. He engineered a meeting at a swimming pool—a dropped towel, a shared laugh. They began an affair, her grief and his curiosity tangled in hotel sheets.

Aaron left Della and told her he did not want the child she was trying to conceive. She wept, but he was already gone.

At the motel, Aaron could not go through with the killing. He only wounded Wes, telling him to run. The bullet caught Wes in the shoulder, blood soaking his work shirt.

Aaron admitted to Lena that he was carrying her husband’s heart. She threw him out, then took him back, her need for something to hold stronger than her rage.

Wes followed the pair back to their motel. He asked Aaron to finish the job. Instead, Aaron turned the gun on himself and pulled the trigger.

Lena and Wes got the dying Aaron to a hospital. The transplanted heart failed. Wes went home to his family, and Lena, pregnant, went home alone.

The tarp had been knotted at the ankles and wrists, the way cargo gets tied. Detective Isaiah Reece knelt in the roadside gravel and loosened it with numb fingers. The face underneath was his brother Kwame. He'd known it before he pulled the tarp back, the way you know your own reflection in a broken mirror. He'd been a detective for eleven years. He had never once gone looking for his brother.

Months earlier, in a fluorescent gun shop, an immigrant named Nadir and his daughter Sahar had bought a handgun while the clerk mimicked Nadir's accent. Sahar paid in cash.

The same Kwame, still alive, had helped Trey carjack a prosecutor's car outside a restaurant. They'd taken Halstead's keys and left him shouting on the sidewalk.

A locksmith named Mateo changed the Halsteads' locks that afternoon. Paula, Mrs. Halstead, stood over him and said her keys were probably already being sold to a gang. Mateo said nothing, handed her the invoice.

On the highway, Officer Boyle pulled over the Hobarts. He made Renee step out, patted her down too long, called her sweetheart. Clay stood at the window with his hands empty while Boyle let them go with a warning.

Later, Voss asked the commander for a different partner. Said he wouldn't ride with a racist. The commander made a note and did nothing.

Mateo replaced the lock on Nadir's shop door too. He said, "The door's rotten, man. A lock won't hold." Nadir accused him of running a con. Mateo shrugged and handed him the key.

Across town, Boyle was on his knees in an insurance office, begging Delia Frank to approve treatment for his father. She said the policy didn't cover it. He left his cap on the desk.

That night, Nadir's shop was smashed and looted. The insurer found the claims report and the warning on file. They denied him. The door was the reason.

Trey and Kwame ran down a shopkeeper named Pham with the stolen car. They stopped just long enough to dump him outside a hospital like a sack of trash.

Renee Hobart was trapped upside down in a burning wreck when Boyle crawled in through the glass and dragged her out by the harness straps. She coughed smoke and said nothing. He was the same man who'd groped her.

Clay Hobart was stopped mid-carjacking of his own car, hands on the door handle, a knife in his fist. Voss held up a hand and talked the other officers down. "He's just a man trying to get home," he said. They let Clay go.

The snow globe hit the marble floor of Silvermount's great hall and did not break. Emmett Rusk was already gone, his last breath shaped around a word no one in the room—and there was no one in the room—could hear. The glass sphere rolled to a stop against a mirror's base, and the tiny white flakes inside continued their silent drift around a miniature sled.

The newsreel called him a titan of industry, a self-made man, a civic benefactor. It showed the Clarion's presses, the opera house he built, the half-finished palace, the governor's race he lost. It closed on his last word—"Bluebell"—and offered no explanation. The theater went dark.

Nash found Nora Rusk in a seaside nightclub, gin-sour and glitter-eyed, and she laughed at him through the smoke. "Bluebell," she said, tasting the word like something spoiled. "You want Bluebell? Go dig him up and ask." She turned away, and the bouncer's hand landed on Nash's shoulder.

He did the next best thing. He read Barrow's memoir, yellowed and self-serving. He sat across from Marsh, who remembered the boy; from Devlin, who remembered the review; from Colm the butler, who remembered the silence.

The memoir said: In a mining boarding house out west, a widow named Rusk signed her nine-year-old son over to the banker Barrow in exchange for the deed to a defaulted lodger's mine. The mine made the family rich. The boy made Barrow's life miserable. On the day of the signing, Emmett drove his sled straight into the banker's soft stomach, and Barrow, wheezing, took him east anyway.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett took control of the fortune. He stood in Barrow's office and said, "Of all your holdings, I want the Clarion." He moved into the newsroom, installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. He hired away the rival paper's entire staff and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line. He went abroad and came back engaged to Adele, the governor's niece.

The breakfast-table scenes went quiet. Separate newspapers, separate silences. He met Nora Kell on the street with mud on his coat and began visiting her rooms in secret. Mid-campaign, Halloran brought Adele to Nora's door and threatened exposure. Emmett refused to withdraw. He lost. Devlin asked for a transfer. Adele left.

He married Nora anyway. He forced her into an opera career for which she had no voice. Her debut was a humiliation. Devlin, drunk, began a savage review; Emmett finished it, printed it, and fired him. Nora swallowed poison. Emmett finally let her stop singing.

He shut her away in Silvermount, the half-finished palace, where she worked jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall. A joyless beach picnic. A quarrel. She packed and left.

Emmett wrecked her bedroom. In the wreckage he found a glass snow globe, lifted it, and murmured "Bluebell." He carried it past the endless mirrors.

Nash closed the memoir. He interviewed them all—Marsh, Devlin, Nora, Colm—and each gave him a different piece of the same man. No single word explained a life, he wrote. Behind him, workmen shoveled a child's sled, painted with the name Bluebell, into the furnace. The flames took the letters one by one, and the word went up with them, unclaimed.

In a flat overlooking the street, an old man was explaining to a younger one that nothing survives time. Dust motes floated in the shaft of light from the window, and the younger man watched the police below handcuff Cort and Jonah, then carry them out of the club. The old man’s voice was dry as ash. “Memory, flesh, even the concrete—all of it crumbles.”

Inside the club, Jonah had beaten a man’s face in with a fire extinguisher while the real Adder watched from a few feet away. The metal rang against bone, and the man’s fingers had already let go of Cort’s snapped arm. Cort had seized the wrong man in his hunt through the club, and the real Adder had broken his arm before melting back into the crowd.

Two men in the street had offered to sell Cort the rapist’s name. They steered him and Jonah towards a club called the Pit. Cort’s knuckles were still white from the ambulance doors. He and Jonah had come out of the party to find Lise being loaded into an ambulance. The paramedics’ gloves were red. The sirens were already fading.

Earlier, in the underpass, the Adder had raped Lise and beaten her head against the concrete. A passer-by glimpsed them and backed away. Lise had taken the pedestrian underpass rather than cross the busy road. She had walked in on the pimp known as the Adder beating a transsexual woman. The woman’s mouth was a dark O of pain. Lise had tried to turn, but the Adder’s hand was already in her hair.

Before that, at the party, Cort had gotten steadily drunk and high. He started pursuing other women, and a disgusted Lise left on her own. She walked out into the night, away from the bass and the laughter. The air was cool. She didn’t know yet that the underpass was the only way home.

On the underground, Lise, Cort, and Jonah had ridden to the party, arguing cheerfully about sex and about Cort’s drinking. The train lurched. Cort’s breath smelled of whiskey. Jonah laughed and said Lise was too good for him. Lise rolled her eyes. The lights flickered.

In bed, Lise lay with Cort describing a recurring dream of a red tunnel. She said it was like being born, but backwards. Cort teased her about her ex-boyfriend Jonah, and she threw a pillow at him. “You’re the one who brings him up,” she said. Cort grinned. “Because you never do.” She traced the line of his jaw. “The tunnel is tight and warm, and then it opens into a room with no windows.”

Alone in the flat, Lise took a pregnancy test. The stick showed a plus sign. She stared at it for a long time, then set it on the edge of the sink. The tiles were cold under her bare feet. She didn’t tell anyone.

In the park, among sprinklers and playing children, Lise sat on a bench with a book. One hand rested on her stomach. The water arced and sparkled. A child ran past, shrieking with joy. Lise didn’t look up from the page, but her fingers pressed gently against the fabric of her dress. The sun was warm. The grass was green. Nothing had happened yet.

The stairwell stank of concrete dust and ozone. Rex was below me, his face a pale smear in the half-light, and I understood with a clarity that felt like the first true thing I'd known in years that he was me. I put the gun in my mouth. The metal was cold, tasted of oil. I pulled the trigger.

But to understand how I got there, you have to go back. I was an insomniac, a product-recall investigator, and the only thing that let me sleep was crying at support groups for diseases I didn't have. The release was real, the grief was borrowed, but it worked. Then Ada Vey started attending the same groups. Her faking was so obvious, so theatrical, it destroyed the careful fiction of my own. I couldn't cry anymore. I couldn't sleep.

On a business flight, I met a soap salesman named Rex Marrow. I pocketed his card, a reflex. Days later, my flat and all my catalogue furniture were destroyed in an explosion. With nowhere else to go, I called the number. Rex took me into a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district.

Outside a bar, he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We beat each other bloody in the car park, and the pain was a language I finally spoke. What started as a brawl hardened into a weekly basement club with its own rules. It pulled in more and more members.

Then Ada overdosed. Rex brought her back to the house, and they began a loud affair I couldn't stand. To fund it all, he rendered fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap, selling it back to department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He burned my hand with lye once, holding me there, refusing to let me retreat into meditation. I blackmailed my employer into paying me to stay away, using my own beaten face as evidence.

Rex turned the club into an organisation he called Havoc, filling the house with shaven recruits who took orders and vandalised corporate property. Then, one night, he steered the car into oncoming traffic, let it roll, and disappeared. A member named Ogden was shot dead on an operation, and I started trying to shut the whole thing down.

Travelling city to city, I found identical clubs everywhere, and men who greeted me as Rex Marrow. I worked out that we were the same person—that Rex had been acting while I slept. Ada confirmed it. She had been sleeping with me, not with a separate man.

I discovered Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies. I tried to defuse the charges. That's how I ended up on the stairwell, with Rex beating me down. I put the gun in my mouth and shot myself through the cheek to kill him.

The blast was a white sun. I woke on the landing, my jaw a ruin, Rex gone. The recruits delivered Ada to the tower. She took my hand, and we stood at the window as the buildings came down around us, the glass shivering, the world falling away into a cloud of white dust that looked, from where we stood, almost like snow.

The helicopters came at dusk, their rotors churning the humid air as they swept across every neighborhood, dousing the city in a fine chemical mist. Inside the Hartigan house, Doctor Neil adjusted his tie while his wife Bess, still smelling of turpentine, dabbed paint from her cuticles. They were late for their own dinner party.

Across town, Cheryl took a deep breath and spoke into the phone in a low, practiced voice. Her husband Stu sat on the couch beside her, fists clenched, listening to her soothe some stranger’s fantasies. In a club downtown, the singer Vida closed her eyes under the spotlight, her voice rising above the clink of glasses. At home, her daughter Bee sat alone in the dark, drawing a bow across her cello, the notes thin and lonely.

Officer Rowe pulled the car over on a deserted road and opened the door. The dog whined, confused. He drove away without looking back, already dialing Nan’s number to explain why he was late.

That morning, Charlie Rill had been knocked down by a waitress named Rhona. He’d gotten up, refused a ride, and walked home saying he was fine. The baker Otto Kemp took the order for his birthday cake—a chocolate layer with blue icing—and wrote “Happy Birthday Charlie” in careful script. By evening, Charlie was in a coma. Grant and Elaine sat in hospital chairs, holding each other’s hands.

Ike and Dot were house-sitting for the Hartigans. Dot lay on the marble floor while Ike arranged her limbs, smearing ketchup on her face. He clicked the camera. “Perfect,” he said.

Stu and three friends drove out to the river. They found a young woman’s body floating face down. Cass, Nan’s ex, learned she had a new man. He took a saw to her dining table, her chairs, her bed. Otto, unpaid and ignored, began making calls. He didn’t say much—just heavy breathing, then a click. The men tethered the body to the bank with rope and continued fishing for two more days.

At the hospital, Duff appeared. Grant’s estranged father, stooped and gray, confessed an affair that had ended decades ago. Grant stared at the floor. Vern’s wife Iris, dressed in her clown costume, scrubbed her face when she heard what the men had done. “Animals,” she whispered.

At the dinner party, Bess drank too much wine. She told Neil about the nude modeling session years ago, and the affair that followed. Neil stood up, knocking over a vase. The guests fell silent.

Charlie died. Grant and Elaine walked to the bakery, ready to scream at Otto. But he opened the door with flour on his hands, pulled out a tray of warm bread, and sat with them. They wept together.

Bee found her mother asleep on the couch. She walked to the garage, closed the door, and started the car. The engine hummed. Vida never woke up.

Stu drove to the hills for a picnic. He saw a young woman gathering wildflowers. He picked up a rock.

A tremor rolled through the city. Windows rattled. The helicopters wobbled and veered. In every home, every hospital, every riverbank, the ground shifted. That night, the evening bulletin folded every death and every wreck into one long, flat list, read by a woman with a steady voice.

Solly Two Coats and his crew, dressed as devout pilgrims, walked out of a diamond house in a northern port with a stone the size of a child’s fist. They were already halfway across the sea when, back in the city, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent the fighter Pretty Sam to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers. Sam haggled poorly, and the bare-knuckle fighter Finn knocked him out cold over the deal. Halloway was left without a man for the fixed bout gang boss Coldstone had arranged.

Overseas, Solly’s cousin Marv sent word: bring the stone straight over. Meanwhile, Halloway had no choice but to put Finn in the fight, promising Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth round. Grigor the Nail, a man with his fingers in every pie, told Solly about a bookmaker’s in the city where a man could bet big—and simultaneously tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to rob him there.

Solly landed, delivered the stone to the fence Hersch, and headed for the bookmaker’s to bet on the fight. But in the ring, Finn knocked his opponent out cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and took it out on Halloway with a beating that left him bloody. Then Ike, Benno, and Tulley bungled the robbery at the bookmaker’s—they took Solly’s arm and his case, but were chased off by Grigor before they could finish the job.

Marv flew in, found Solly gone, and hired the bounty hunter Ledge to find him. Grigor took Solly, cut off his arm to get the case open, and found the stone was not inside. Coldstone fed Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong. So Ledge traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces, and took both them and the stone. Halloway and Digby told Finn to go down in the fourth, and Coldstone’s men burned Finn’s mother to death in her caravan.

Grigor ambushed Ledge’s car with Ike and Benno inside. In the shootout, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. But Tulley got away with the dog that had swallowed the diamond. In the ring, Finn knocked his opponent out again in the fourth round, and the travellers—who had come for revenge—massacred Coldstone’s men in the crowd. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone and shot him. By morning, the travellers had vanished.

The dog was handed in at a pet shop. It coughed up the diamond, and Halloway and Digby ended up holding it—a stone that had passed through too many hands, now sitting quiet in theirs.

The coffee shop smelled of stale grease and burnt coffee. Two men in cheap jackets sat in a red vinyl booth, nursing cups they hadn't touched. They were small-time, thinking small-time thoughts. One of them, wiry and twitchy, looked at the register, then at the bored cashier, then back at his partner. "We could do it now," he said. The partner, heavier, slower, blinked. "Here?" The wiry one was already standing, hand inside his jacket. "Right here."

Across town, a black sedan crawled through traffic. Rollo drove with one hand, gesturing with the other. "In Amsterdam, you can buy it in a coffee shop. Legal." Marcus, in the passenger seat, shook his head. "That's not a coffee shop, that's a—" He stopped. "You know what they call a Big Mac in France? A Royal with Cheese." The argument died as they parked, their attention narrowing to the job at hand.

They stood in a dim corridor, outside a flat. Rollo leaned against the wall, checking his weapon. "You ever get a foot massage? I'm asking if it's worth killing a man for." Marcus didn't look up from his gun. "It's a job. The money's the point." They moved before the answer could come.

Inside, a young man named Tobin stood by a table, a briefcase at his feet. He saw them and his face went pale. Marcus recited a line of scripture, his voice low and even, and then the room erupted. Two shots. Tobin crumpled. Marcus took the briefcase. A fourth man burst from the bathroom, a revolver in his hand, firing wildly. Five shots, all missing. Marcus looked at Rollo, a ghost of a smile on his face. "Divine intervention."

They delivered the briefcase to Otis at his bar. Otis didn't look at them, just nodded at the case. He was talking to an ageing boxer named Denny, a man with scarred knuckles and tired eyes. "Fifth round, Denny. You go down in the fifth." Denny nodded, but his eyes were on the briefcase.

Later, Rollo bought heroin from his dealer, Kip. He shot up in the car, then took Otis's wife, Nadia, to a themed diner. They won the dance contest, laughing, spinning under cheap lights. Back at Kip's, Nadia snorted some of Rollo's stash. Her eyes rolled back. She stopped breathing. Kip slammed an adrenaline shot into her heart, and she gasped back to life, Rollo watching with a strange, detached calm.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war had handed a young boy a gold watch. "Your father kept this hidden for four years. He wanted you to have it." The boy, Denny, had held it, feeling the weight of a promise.

Now, Denny stood in a ring, the roar of the crowd in his ears. He was supposed to fall in the fifth. Instead, he threw a right cross that connected with a sickening crunch, and his opponent went down, not getting up. He escaped in a taxi, a dead man walking. At a motel, his girlfriend Marielle was packing. "Denny, your father's watch. You left it at your flat." He went back for it.

He found Rollo in his kitchen, surprised. Rollo reached for a submachine gun left on the counter. Denny was faster. The gun stuttered, and Rollo fell. Denny grabbed the watch and ran. In the street, he collided with Otis's car. They crashed, and were dragged to a pawnshop basement, prisoners.

Denny broke free. He tore a sword from the shop wall, its blade catching the light. One of their captors was on top of Otis. Denny swung the flat of the blade, sending the man sprawling. Otis looked up, bloodied, and nodded. "We're square. Just leave town." Denny collected Marielle, took a motorcycle from the shop, and rode out of the city.

Back in the sedan, Rollo's gun went off. The bullet took off the head of their passenger, Del. Marcus swore as he pulled over, parking the bloodied car at his friend Warren's house. A fixer directed the cleanup, handing them fresh clothes. They drove to a coffee shop. Marcus walked in and found himself facing a nervous man with a gun. The small-time robber. Marcus talked him down, handed over his wallet, and kept the briefcase. The couple walked out, the robbery over. Marcus sat down, ordered coffee, and waited for the world to catch up.

He was conscripted as a chaplain’s assistant and shipped overseas with no training worth the name. The chaplain was a fat man who prayed for victory and drank from a flask. The boy—he was still a boy then—carried the hymnal and the communion kit, and he learned to keep his head down.

He is taken by aliens and kept in a zoo on their planet with a film actress. She had been missing for three years, and now she sat on the plastic grass and wept. The aliens were tall and silent. They watched through the glass. One day they explained that every moment exists at once and that free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet. He tried to understand, but the actress kept weeping.

He was born in a small industrial town and grew into a weak, peculiar child. The mills belched smoke. His mother died when he was four. His father was a foreman with hands like bricks. The boy read books about invisible men and lost worlds.

He is sent on to a great city and housed with other prisoners in a disused abattoir. The hooks still swung from the ceiling. They slept on concrete stained with old blood. The war was over for them, but no one came to tell them.

He comes home, collapses, and is hospitalised. The ward smells of iodine and boiled cabbage. Another patient introduces him to a hack science fiction writer who wears a bow tie and talks about the fourth dimension. The writer gives him a book inscribed with the words: *Time is a river, but you can step in it twice.*

The aliens say every moment exists at once. He remembers the scout who beat him for wanting to be left to die. They were lost behind the lines. The scout’s knuckles split his lip. *Get up, you coward.* He got up.

He marries the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school and becomes rich. He wears suits now. His wife’s father dies and leaves him the business. He has a daughter who grows up in a house with a swimming pool. He never swims in it.

The city is destroyed by fire in one night. The prisoners in the meat locker come up to find it gone. The sky is orange. The streets are rivers of glass. They stand in the smoke and do not know what to do.

His daughter decides he is senile and takes his affairs out of his hands. She finds the science fiction books, the notes about aliens. She calls a lawyer. He sits in the garden and watches the birds.

His father threw him into the deep end of a pool to teach him to swim. He sank to the bottom. The water was green and cold. He opened his eyes and saw the light above him. He did not try to rise. His father pulled him out by the hair and hit him.

The pair are captured, and the scout dies of gangrene on the prison train, blaming him with his last breath. *You did this. You.* The scout’s face was grey. The train rattled on. He did not answer.

He goes on a radio talk show and tries to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension. The host cuts him off. The callers laugh. He says, *Time is a loop. I have seen it.* They play a commercial.

The prisoners are made to dig bodies out of the cellars until one of the diggers dies of the dry heaves. The bodies are black and swollen. The digger falls over, and no one stops digging.

He survives an air crash in the mountains, and his wife dies of exhaust fumes driving to the hospital. He walks away from the wreckage. The snow is red. He finds her in the car at the bottom of the ravine. The engine is still running.

He is held in a camp beside enemy officers who have been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error. They are fat and polished. They play chess. He watches them and thinks of the scout.

He is shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd, exactly as he has always known he would be. The beam is silent. He falls. The crowd scatters. The aliens were right: every moment exists at once, and he has been here all along.

A fellow prisoner promises to have him killed one day on the dead scout’s account. The man’s name is something he forgets. The man points a finger at him. *I’ll find you.* He nods. He knows it’s true.

Two years later, in a bar that smelled of spilled ale and old wood, Odile found Wilder again. She looked thinner, her eyes carrying a weight that hadn’t been there when they’d shared linen and plates and a quiet district’s stillness. She told him her marriage was over. The previous night, she said, she had confessed everything to Emlyn—every afternoon in those rented rooms, every hour they’d stolen while the world assumed otherwise. Wilder said nothing, just watched the amber light in her glass.

Then she let slip the other thing. Emlyn had been publishing a writer whom Wilder represented, a man they both quietly detested, whose prose they’d mocked over wine and whose success felt like a personal insult. Wilder’s hand tightened around his glass. The betrayal was no longer merely domestic; it had crept into his work, his name, his livelihood.

He rang Emlyn that same evening, his voice frayed and sharp. Emlyn came to his house before the night had fully settled. He stood in the doorway, coat still on, face unreadable. And then he spoke. He had known for four years. His wife had told him on the trip abroad, in that hotel where a letter had waited at the desk. He never thought much of his friend’s letters either. The words landed like stones in still water.

Long before that, there had been the decision to end it. The rented rooms had become a chore, a burden of secrecy rather than a refuge. They split the crockery—a set of blue-rimmed plates, a mismatched collection of cups—and surrendered the lease. The affair had its own household, and now it had its own funeral.

And before that, there was the dinner at the married couple’s house. The two men had talked of racquet games and schoolboy sport, their voices easy and loud, while Odile sat silent, excluded from a conversation that seemed designed to erase her. She had no part in it at all.

Further back, in a hotel abroad, Emlyn had asked about a letter held for her at the desk. The handwriting was familiar to him. She had confessed then, and he had remarked—with a strange, almost gentle detachment—that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife. She had returned to the rented rooms afterward and said nothing whatever about the trip. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had, as if the confession had never happened.

Before that, Emlyn had drunk through a long restaurant lunch with Wilder, baiting him about contemporary fiction, never once mentioning what he had learned. The meal had stretched on, a performance of normalcy, while the truth sat between them like an uninvited guest.

And at the beginning, before the weight of it all, Wilder and Odile had rented rooms in a quiet district. They filled them with linen and plates, giving the affair a household of its own. She told him she was carrying her husband’s child, and they decided the rooms would go on exactly as before.

But the true beginning was a party at the house of Wilder’s closest friend. The other guests drank downstairs, their laughter muffled by the floorboards. Wilder led Odile to an upstairs room and told her how lovely she was. That was the first stone, the one that started the avalanche. Everything else—the rooms, the confessions, the silences—was just the fall.

The train smelled of salt and diesel, and Tobias did not know why he was on it. He had woken with a vacancy in his chest, a skipped beat he could not name, and instead of going to work he had bought a ticket to the end of the line. The sea appeared between the dunes, gray and indifferent. He walked to the beach. The sand was frozen, crunching under his shoes. A woman stood at the waterline, her coat whipping in the wind. She turned when he approached, as if she had been waiting.

“You came,” she said. Her name was Ivy, and he did not know her, and yet something in him tilted toward her like a compass finding north.

They drove back to the city in silence, the heater humming. She invited him up to her flat. He went.

---

Two days before, Tobias had walked into a bookshop and seen Ivy laughing with a young man named Peck, her hand on his arm, her eyes bright with the terrible ease of a stranger. She had looked through Tobias as if he were made of glass. He had stood in the stacks, breathing shallow, and watched her flirt.

That night, Nina and Grady showed him the form letter from the clinic. PROCEDURE COMPLETE. PATIENT NO LONGER REPORTS ASSOCIATED MEMORIES. He had gone to Dr. Hallam’s office the next morning and demanded the same.

He boxed everything: the photographs, the scarf she had left, the ticket stubs from the drive-in, the smooth stone from the frozen river. The technicians Dell and Peck set up their equipment in his flat. Peck’s fingers lingered on the mementos, sliding one into his pocket when he thought no one was looking.

Inside his own head, Tobias watched the memories dissolve. The ugliest went first: the dented car, her slurred accusations, his own cold silence. He felt them peel away like scabs. Then the older ones began to fray—the noodle house, the ice cracking under their boots—and panic seized him. He tried to force his way into memories he had never been part of, to hide her in corners where she had never stood, to smuggle her into his childhood, his first job, anywhere she might survive.

The procedure went off the rails. Dell and Rosa got high on his bed, giggling, losing track of the map. Dr. Hallam arrived to re-map the erasure, and Rosa kissed him, and his wife appeared in the doorway and said, quietly, that Rosa’s own affair with him had been erased months ago. The room went still.

In the last surviving memory, Tobias stood in the empty house on the shore, the one they had broken into at the end of the rail line. Ivy was there, younger, softer. She said goodbye, and she told him to meet her at the beach.

The erasure completed.

---

Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy had ever existed. He skipped work on an impulse he could not account for. He took the train to the coast.

---

Rosa quit the clinic that week. She mailed the files and session tapes back to every patient on the books, unmarked envelopes sliding through mail slots across the city. Tobias and Ivy received one. They sat on her couch and listened to their own recorded voices tearing each other apart—her slurred apologies, his clipped refusals, the sound of a door slamming.

Ivy ran. She came back. She stood in the doorway, breathless, and said, “We could try anyway.”

Tobias looked at her. He did not know her. He knew her. The vacancy in his chest had a name after all.

“Okay,” he said.
